stories.summary: Researchers at the U of A and the University of Michigan have reported the creation of a graphene-based energy harvester that uses ambient radiation to run temperature sensors that use very little electricity. Thibado noted that ambient radiation is everywhere in modern life, especially radiating from the electrical wiring of our homes (though the wires running through the walls could be better arranged to take advantage of this waste radiation). The temperature sensor systems created by Thibado's group focused on the standard 60 Hertz electrical frequency commonly used in the U.S. The sensor uses a graphene inductor to harvest energy from the magnetic fields created by these power lines.
stories.editorialText: Researchers at the U of A and the University of Michigan have reported the creation of a graphene-based energy harvester that uses ambient radiation to run ultra-low-power temperature sensors. This is the second sensor created by the team whose overall goal is development of autonomous sensor systems that draw power from multiple sources in the environment — solar, thermal, acoustic, kinetic, nonlinear and ambient radiation. The team previously reported successful development of graphene-based solar cells that can be used to power temperature sensors. The team has three requirements for these sensors: they must use locally harvested energy, they must have a long unattended service life (potentially decades) and they must be able to operate at nanowatt-scale power. All three requirements have been met in the latest sensor utilizing ambient radiation. MD Rezaul Kabir, a Ph.D. candidate in the Materials Science and Engineering Program at the U of A, was first author on the paper, but graphene energy harvesters are the invention of U of A physics professor Paul Thibado, who began studying graphene's unique properties more than a decade ago

(AP) — Portions of a Mississippi ban on diversity, equity and inclusion practices in public schools can go into effect after the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower court’s ruling that blocked sections of the law from being enforced. The parts of the law in question prevent public schools from requiring diversity training and maintaining DEI-related programs, courses and offices. reserveStories.editorialText: Researchers at the U of A and the University of Michigan have reported the creation of a graphene-based energy harvester that uses ambient radiation to run ultra-low-power temperature sensors. This is the second sensor created by the team whose overall goal is development of autonomous sensor systems that draw power from multiple sources in the environment — solar, thermal, acoustic, kinetic, nonlinear and ambient radiation. The team previously reported successful development of graphene-based solar cells that can be used to power temperature sensors. The team has three requirements for these sensors: they must use locally harvested energy, they must have a long unattended service life (potentially decades) and they must be able to operate at nanowatt-scale power. All three requirements have been met in the latest sensor utilizing ambient radiation. MD Rezaul Kabir, a Ph.D. candidate in the Materials Science and Engineering Program at the U of A, was first author on the paper, but graphene energy harvesters are the invention of U of A physics professor Paul Thibado, who began studying graphene's unique properties more than a decade ago

(AP) — Portions of a Mississippi ban on diversity, equity and inclusion practices in public schools can go into effect after the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower court’s ruling that blocked sections of the law from being enforced. The parts of the law in question prevent public schools from requiring diversity training and maintaining DEI-related programs, courses and offices. reserveStories.summary: MIAMI (AP) — A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11. The order from U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett came as lawyers for the British broadcaster complained that Trump had delayed his appearance in his own lawsuit. Charles Tobin, attorney for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.” Meanwhile, it remained uncertain whether former special counsel Jack Smith would be allowed to sit for a deposition. Federal rules require current and former employees to receive permission from agency heads before testifying in court cases.
reserveStories.editorialText: MIAMI (AP) — A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11. The order from U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett came as lawyers for the British broadcaster complained that Trump had delayed his appearance in his own lawsuit. Charles Tobin, attorney for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.” Meanwhile, it remained uncertain whether former special counsel Jack Smith would be allowed to sit for a deposition. Federal rules require current and former employees to receive permission from agency heads before testifying in court cases. Smith has requested permission but has not received an answer, and the judge ruled that the department must respond to him by Nov. 2. In arguments about Trump’s deposition, Tobin noted there had been an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, but Trump had canceled it for a “matter of national importance.” He said the Republican president was in fact campaigning in Georgia that day.
